teaser: He only ever showed the left side of his face. There was a reason.
review_notes:
Federico da Montefeltro lost his right eye and damaged his nose in a tournament in 1450. The 'surgery to widen his field of vision' story is presented as legend.
Battista Sforza married at 13 (1460), bore several daughters, then Guidobaldo in January 1472, and died in July 1472 aged 26. Her portrait is widely thought to be posthumous, possibly from a death mask: presented as likely, not certain.
Federico became Duke only in 1474; the diptych is usually dated c. 1472-1475 (metadata says 1472).
Each panel about 47 x 33 cm.
Reverse sides: triumphal chariots, Federico crowned by Victory, Battista's chariot drawn by unicorns, with Latin inscriptions (not visible in this image).
The diptych came to Florence in 1631 with the della Rovere inheritance.
Normal placement of husband on the left in paired portraits, reversed here: common observation.

lesson.text: Do you have a good side, the one you turn toward the camera? Federico da Montefeltro, ruler of Urbino, had one too, and he never let a painter see the other. Every known portrait shows him exactly like this: facing left, in strict profile.

In 1450, at a tournament, a lance slipped through his visor. It destroyed his right eye and smashed the bridge of his nose. He was 28 and made his living as a soldier. He survived, went back to war, and from then on the left side of his face was the official one.

A stubborn legend says Federico had surgeons cut away the bridge of his nose so that his remaining eye could see across it and no assassin could approach from the blind side. More likely the lance did the job by itself.

The profile had a second advantage. It is how emperors appear on ancient Roman coins, and Italian princes of the 1400s adored that comparison. Paired portraits normally put the husband on the left, the place of honor. Here the couple had to swap, so that Federico could face his wife.

She is Battista Sforza. She married him at 13, read Latin, and governed Urbino during his long campaigns. In 1472, a few months after giving birth to the son the couple had waited years for, she died at 26. Her wax-pale face suggests Piero painted her after her death, as a memorial.
The two panels are small, each about 47 by 33 centimeters (18.5 by 13 inches), and a strip of frame separates them. Yet Piero ties them together in two ways that you sense before you notice.
Two lines cross the gap between the panels.

lines.label: One horizon
lines.text: The pale blue line of far hills runs at the same height behind both heads. It is a single country, continuing behind the frame as if the frame were a window post.

lines.label: Eye to eye
lines.text: Their eyes sit at almost the same level, fixed on each other across the divide. Neither glances at us. If she was already dead, this steady look is all the more moving.

lesson.text: That landscape is half the message. We see it from high up, level with two giants who look down on the land they govern. The hills get paler and bluer as they recede, the way real distance looks through air, an effect called aerial perspective. Piero learned to do it with oil paint, a slow-drying medium then arriving from northern Europe that allows soft, see-through layers.

Federico paid for his palace, his painters and one of the largest libraries in Italy by renting out his army. He was a condottiere, a general for hire, and cities paid him handsomely to fight for them, or sometimes simply not to fight against them.

The two faces are painted by different rules. His is a map of every flaw. Hers is smooth as an egg, with wealth pinned and stitched all over it. The details show how a prince and a princess were each expected to look.

spots.title: The broken nose
spots.text: The bridge of the nose drops in a sharp notch below the brow, the scar of the tournament. Piero outlines it crisply against the sky. Federico turned the injury into a trademark.

spots.title: Moles and creases
spots.text: Dark moles dot the cheek, and lines fold around the mouth and under the eye. Nothing is smoothed away. Honesty was part of the image he wanted: a tough, experienced soldier.

spots.title: A very high forehead
spots.text: Fashionable women plucked or shaved the hairline to lengthen the brow. Battista's forehead curves up to a ribbon near the top of her skull, pale and unlined.

spots.title: Jewel and ribbons
spots.text: A brooch of gold, pearls and blue stones sits over her ear, with hair coiled around white ribbons beside it. Piero paints each strand and loop as if counting them.

spots.title: Pearls
spots.text: A jeweled collar and a long rope of pearls, each bead given its own tiny highlight and shadow. Pearls stood for purity, and they also stated the price of the necklace quite clearly.

spots.title: Two boats
spots.text: Small sailboats sit on a glassy river, each with its reflection. This quiet water behind a warlord's shoulder says: under my rule, there is peace and trade.

spots.title: A walled town
spots.text: A pale line of walls and towers lies in the plain behind Battista. Her side of the land is settled and fortified, a hint at the regent who kept the state running.

spots.title: The red hat
spots.text: A flat-topped red cap and a plain red coat, no gold, no chain, no armor. Against the pale sky the color alone gives him the weight of a monument.

lesson.text: There is more painting on the back. Turn the panels over and each spouse rides a triumphal chariot through the same kind of landscape, hers pulled by unicorns, with Latin verses praising them underneath.
A portrait can hide half a face and still feel truthful. Piero shows only what the duke allowed, then records that half without flattery, and lets a wide, calm landscape speak for the rest.

quiz.question: Why is Federico always shown from the left?
options: Court painters only knew how to draw profiles
He lost his right eye in a tournament
The left was considered the unlucky side
quiz.explanation: A lance destroyed his right eye in 1450, so the left side became his official face.

quiz.question: Which ancient objects did the profile format recall?
quiz.explanation: Emperors appear in profile on Roman coins, a flattering comparison for a prince.

quiz.question: What links the two separate panels?
options: A shared inscription across the top
A chain held by both sitters
A continuous landscape with a single horizon
quiz.explanation: The same line of distant hills runs behind both heads.

quiz.question: What is aerial perspective?
options: Making distant things paler and bluer
quiz.explanation: The hills fade toward blue as they recede, like real distance seen through air.

quiz.question: How did Federico earn his fortune?
quiz.explanation: He was a condottiere who rented out his army to Italian states.

facts.text: Battista Sforza outlived her husband by many years.
facts.explanation: She died in 1472 at 26, soon after the birth of their son.

facts.text: The backs of the two panels are painted as well.
facts.explanation: Each shows one spouse riding a triumphal chariot, with Latin verses.

facts.text: Piero smoothed away the moles and wrinkles on Federico's face.
facts.explanation: He recorded them carefully, as the marks of an experienced soldier.
